Somewhat
SUM-hwut
n., adv.
From some plus what. Webster 1828 gives both a noun sense — something, more or less — and an adverbial one, in some degree. The KJV keeps the noun, now nearly extinct in English: I have somewhat to say unto thee means I have a thing to say, not I have a little to say.

Biblical Definition

The KJV’s somewhat is usually a noun, and mistaking it for the modern adverb weakens some of the most serious sentences in Scripture. When our Lord says to His host, Simon, I have somewhat to say unto thee (Luke 7:40), He is not softening the blow; He has a matter to lay before him, and the parable of the two debtors follows. When the risen Christ says to Ephesus, Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love (Revelation 2:4), He is not registering mild dissatisfaction. He has a charge. The Old Testament uses it the same way for guilt incurred unawares: When a ruler hath sinned, and done somewhat through ignorance against any of the commandments of the LORD his God… and is guilty (Leviticus 4:22). Two other uses are worth keeping. Rehoboam’s petitioners ask him to ease somewhat the grievous servitude (2 Chronicles 10:4), where the adverbial sense of degree is genuine. And Paul says of the Jerusalem leaders who seemed to be somewhat that God accepteth no man's person (Galatians 2:6) — to be somewhat is to be somebody, and Paul declines to weigh reputation.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives SOMEWHAT as a noun — something, more or less; a certain quantity or degree — and as an adverb, in some degree or quantity. The KJV’s commonest use is the noun, which modern English has almost entirely lost.

expand to see more

SOMEWHAT, n. — Something, though uncertain what; more or less; a certain quantity or degree, indeterminate.

Also, a person or thing of some importance; as, he thinks himself somewhat.

SOMEWHAT, adv. — In some degree or quantity; as, somewhat larger.

Both senses stand in the KJV. Luke 7:40 and Revelation 2:4 are the noun — a matter, a charge; 2 Chronicles 10:4 is the adverb of degree; and Galatians 2:6 is Webster’s second noun sense, a person of reputed importance.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 4:22 — "When a ruler hath sinned, and done somewhat through ignorance against any of the commandments of the LORD his God concerning things which should not be done, and is guilty;"

Luke 7:40 — "And Jesus answering said unto him, Simon, I have somewhat to say unto thee. And he saith, Master, say on."

Revelation 2:4 — "Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love."

Galatians 2:6 — "But of these who seemed to be somewhat, (whatsoever they were, it maketh no matter to me: God accepteth no man's person:) for they who seemed to be somewhat in conference added nothing to me:"

2 Chronicles 10:4 — "Thy father made our yoke grievous: now therefore ease thou somewhat the grievous servitude of thy father, and his heavy yoke that he put upon us, and we will serve thee."

Modern Corruption

The corruption is a misreading with real consequences: taking the noun for the adverb turns Christ’s charge against Ephesus into a mild complaint, and turns Leviticus 4:22 from guilt into a trifle.

expand to see more

Revelation 2:4 is the verse that suffers most. Read as the modern adverb, I have somewhat against thee sounds like a minor reservation appended to a commendation, and it is preached that way — a church doing well with a small area for growth. The English of 1611 will not carry that. Christ has a matter against Ephesus, and the following verse gives the sentence: Repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place. That is the removal of a church, and it is what the somewhat introduces. A church that has kept its doctrine, its discipline, and its patience, and lost its first love, is under a threat, not a suggestion.

Leviticus 4:22 loses in the other direction. A ruler who hath sinned, and done somewhat through ignorance is guilty — the text says so in the same sentence. Ignorance reduces neither the fact nor the need for a sacrifice; it only changes which offering is brought. The modern instinct that sincerity cancels culpability has no footing here. Guilt in Scripture is a status before God’s law, not a feeling about one’s own conduct, and Leviticus 4 exists precisely because a man can incur it without noticing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Somewhat is an English word, not the rendering of a single Hebrew or Greek lemma; it stands for indefinite pronouns and neuter substantives in both testaments.

expand to see more

English somewhat — Webster 1828, something, more or less; also a person of reputed importance.

Greek ti (G5100) — the indefinite something; behind I have somewhat to say unto thee (Luke 7:40) and I have somewhat against thee (Revelation 2:4).

Greek einai ti — to be something, that is, to be somebody; Galatians 2:6, and compare Galatians 6:3, if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing.

Hebrew 'achath in Leviticus 4:22 is the ordinary one or any one of the commandments; the KJV renders the sense with somewhat.

The modern narrowing of somewhat to a degree-adverb happened after 1611 and is the source of the misreading.

Usage

"Simon, I have somewhat to say unto thee (Luke 7:40) — a matter to lay before a man, not a small remark."

"I have somewhat against thee (Revelation 2:4) — a charge from the risen Christ, answered in the next verse with a threat to remove the candlestick."

"Who seemed to be somewhat (Galatians 2:6) — to be somebody; Paul refuses to weigh reputation because God accepts no man's person."
